direct-pico-guitar.title: Direct-Wired Guitar
direct-pico-guitar.subtitle: Replace a guitar's board with a Pico wired to its frets, strum and whammy
direct-pico-guitar.description: Take the original board out of a Guitar Hero or Rock Band guitar and wire its frets, strum bar, whammy, tilt and buttons straight to a Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2. Works with the original switches or mechanical ones.

intro.title: 1. Getting Started & Standard Pinout
intro.description: Prepare your tools and microcontroller, and review the standard Santroller wiring plan.
intro.familyGh: Guitar Hero (Les Paul, WT, GH5, Xplorer)
intro.welcome: This guide covers converting or rewiring a Guitar Hero or Rock Band controller to a Raspberry Pi Pico or Pico 2.
intro.directRewireCaption: A direct-wired mechanical switch guitar with a Raspberry Pi Pico
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2: Any standard RP2040 or RP2350 board.
Soldering iron & solder: 60/40 or lead-free.
Wire (26-30 AWG): Stranded or solid core wire.
Multimeter: Used in continuity mode (the mode that beeps when probes touch) to trace common grounds and signals.
Wire strippers & cutters: For prepping hookup wires.
rules: Find Common Ground: Use a multimeter in continuity mode to identify shared ground traces or wires.
Trace Signal Wires: Trace signal wires for each switch or potentiometer.
Solder & Verify: Solder to your chosen GP pin, then test.
intro.pinoutDesc: Use the default Santroller pin layout or choose your own GPIO pins.

frets.title: 2. Fret Buttons & Slider
frets.description: Connect the 5 fret buttons (Green, Red, Yellow, Blue, Orange) and optional touch slider bar, then verify each input in real time.
frets.intro: The frets are simple mechanical or membrane switches. Each colour has its own signal wire, and the other side of every switch goes to ground. That makes 6 wires to the Pico: 5 fret signals and 1 ground.
frets.introRb: Wire every fret straight to its own Pico pin. Rock Band necks have two rows of frets, each with its own ground, so this takes 12 wires: 5 upper fret signals + 1 upper ground, and 5 solo fret signals + 1 solo ground. Both grounds go to Pico GND. On a stock neck the solo frets share the 7-wire harness, so you need to run dedicated wires from the lower (solo) fret PCB to the body.
frets.pcbCaption: Example neck PCB (Xplorer): each fret has its own coloured signal trace, while the black ground traces are split across several connector pins
frets.stepGround: Identify Ground: If the neck cable or PCB is not labelled, inspect the neck PCB traces. Ground is not always one trace looping past every switch; as on the Xplorer neck above, it can be split into several traces (black) that each reach their own connector pin.
frets.stepMultimeter: Confirm with Multimeter: In continuity mode, touch one probe to a ground pin and the other to a fret wire. Pressing that fret should beep. Check each fret, as different frets may use different ground pins.
frets.stepSolderGround: Solder Ground: Connect every ground pin from the neck to a GND pin on the Raspberry Pi Pico (e.g., Pin 3 or Pin 8). They can share one GND pin.
frets.stepSolderSignals: Solder Fret Signals: Connect each coloured fret signal wire to an unused digital GPIO pin. Our recommended standard uses:
frets.pullUpText: Santroller automatically configures internal pull-up resistors on the Pico for all digital buttons, so you do not need any external resistors. When you press a fret, it shorts the GP pin to Ground.
frets.benchHint: Assign pins manually or click Probe and press the fret button on your guitar to auto-detect its wiring:
frets.gh5Intro: Guitar Hero 5 necks feature a 4-wire digital bus that communicates over I2C. This carries the 5 fret buttons AND the capacitive touch slider bar over just two data pins plus power with zero neck modifications.
frets.gh5PinGnd: GND → Pico Pin 38 (or any GND pin)
frets.gh5VoltageWarning: Always use 3.3V (Pin 36). Never connect the neck to 5V (VBUS); doing so will permanently damage the neck controller IC.
frets.gh5DriverCardDesc: Enable Santroller's built-in GH5 neck driver to automatically configure I2C on GP{{sda}}/GP{{scl}} and map both the frets and the touch slider bar.
frets.gh5DriverActive: I2C Driver Active (GP{{sda}} SDA / GP{{scl}} SCL)
frets.rbSoloIntro: Stock Rock Band guitars with solo frets use a 7-wire harness: 5 fret signal lines, 1 upper fret common, and 1 solo fret common. Santroller scans this directly as a 5x2 matrix across 5 fret signal columns (GP2-GP6) and 2 row outputs (GP14 Upper, GP15 Solo), reading all 10 frets with no trace cutting required. The neck has no diodes, so holding an upper and a solo fret of the same colour at the same time connects GP14 to GP15 through the two switches while they are scanned: that colour reads unreliably and the two row outputs briefly drive against each other. Avoid holding both frets of one colour, or use the split neck method if you need them together.
frets.rbSoloMatrixNoGnd: Do not connect the neck common wires to Pico GND. The Pico drives them dynamically as matrix row outputs.
frets.rbSoloDriverDesc: Enable Santroller's built-in Matrix driver to configure GP2-GP6 as column inputs and GP14/GP15 as row outputs, mapping all 10 frets automatically.
frets.rbSoloDriverActive: Matrix Driver Active (GP2-GP6 In / GP14-GP15 Out)
frets.rbShiftedIntro: Some 7-pin Rock Band necks share a common Ground with a dedicated Solo switch line. When a solo fret is pressed, it shorts both that fret's signal and the Solo line to Ground. Santroller models this via Shifted Inputs: normal frets trigger when the fret is pressed without Solo, while solo frets trigger when both are pressed.
frets.rbShiftedDriverDesc: Configure all 10 frets automatically using Shifted inputs on GP2-GP6 with GP12 as the Solo modifier.
frets.mpr121Intro: Guitar Hero World Tour guitars used a single-wire analog slider bar with high latency and limited chord detection. Bypassing the stock chip with an MPR121 capacitive touch breakout over I2C provides ultra-low latency multi-touch tracking.
frets.mpr121StepTraces: Cut traces leading away from chip U2 (or desolder U2 entirely) on the slider PCB as shown in the diagram.
frets.mpr121TracesCaption: Trace cuts around U2 on the World Tour slider PCB
frets.mpr121StepVias: Solder wires from each via (channels 0 through 4) on the slider PCB to channels 0-4 on the MPR121 breakout.
frets.mpr121ViasCaption: Slider via locations to solder to MPR121 channels 0-4
frets.mpr121I2cTitle: 3. MPR121 to Raspberry Pi Pico Connections
frets.mpr121StepFrets: The MPR121 only handles the slider. Wire the 5 fret buttons and their ground directly to the Pico (GP2-GP6), exactly as in Direct GPIO mode, and test them in the panel on the right.
frets.mpr121StepI2c: Connect the MPR121 to the Pico over I2C: 3.3V (Pin 36), GND (Pin 38), SDA ({{sdaPin}}), and SCL ({{sclPin}}).
frets.mpr121DriverDesc: Add an MPR121 on I2C (GP{{sda}} SDA / GP{{scl}} SCL) and map its channels 0-4 to the five slider zones.

strum.title: 3. Strum Bar Switches
strum.description: Connect Strum Up and Strum Down switches, cut board traces if reusing original PCBs, and test switch actuation.
strum.intro: The strum bar is operated by two switches: Strum Up and Strum Down. Like the frets, these two switches share a common ground wire.
strum.strumPcbCaption: Strum switches on an original main PCB
strum.directIntro: When using replacement mechanical switches (like Kailh Box switches) or a 3D-printed strum bracket, the switches are completely isolated from stock circuitry.
strum.directStepGround: Common Ground: Connect one pin of each switch together and wire to any GND pin on the Pico.
strum.directStepUp: Strum Up: Connect the signal contact to GP7 (Pin 10).
strum.directStepDown: Strum Down: Connect the signal contact to GP8 (Pin 11).
strum.cutTraceDesc1: If your strum switches are soldered directly to an original console PCB (such as Wii, Xbox 360, or PS3), they remain connected to the original console microcontroller and capacitors. This causes phantom or stuck inputs unless traces are cut.
strum.cutTraceDesc2: Use a craft knife or razor to score and sever the copper traces leading away from the switch pins. Use your multimeter in continuity mode to confirm each switch contact is isolated from the rest of the board.
strum.cutTraceCaption: Cutting copper traces around strum switch contacts
strum.benchHint: Assign pins manually or flick the strum bar to auto-detect the switch:
strum.debounceDesc: Mechanical strum switches can bounce on release, causing unwanted double strums. You can fine-tune Strum Debounce in Profile Poll Settings if you notice accidental over-strums.

whammy.title: 4. Whammy Bar Potentiometer
whammy.description: Wire the 10k potentiometer to 3.3V, Ground, and ADC0 (GP26), then test live analog movement.
whammy.intro: The whammy bar connects to an analog potentiometer (typically 10kΩ). Unlike digital buttons, which are either on or off, the whammy measures variable depth and must connect to one of the Pico's dedicated Analog ADC pins.
whammy.potCenter: Centre Pin (Signal / Wiper): Solder to GP26 (ADC0 / Pin 31) on your Pico.
whammy.potOuter1: Outer Pin 1: Solder to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36) on your Pico.
whammy.potOuter2: Outer Pin 2: Solder to GND (Pin 38) on your Pico.
whammy.invertNote: (Note: If the whammy value decreases when pressed instead of increasing, you can either swap the two outer wires or toggle "Invert" in calibration.)
whammy.warning2WireDesc: Some stock guitars have a potentiometer PCB where two pins are bridged, leaving only 2 wires exposed. You must desolder the bridged connection and solder 3 distinct wires directly to the 3 potentiometer pins.
whammy.warning2WireCaption: Desoldering bridged pins to wire 3 full lines (3V3, Signal, GND)
whammy.pickupIntro: Rock Band Stratocaster and Precision Bass guitars include a 5-way pickup selector switch for guitar effects. Like the whammy, it connects to an analog ADC pin (GP27 / ADC1).
whammy.pickupCenter: Signal / Wiper Pin: Connect to GP27 (ADC1 / Pin 32).
whammy.pickup2WireDesc: On the Rock Band Precision Bass, the pickup potentiometer PCB bridges two pins. Desolder the small attached PCB and run 3 distinct wires directly from the potentiometer pins to 3.3V, GP27, and GND.
whammy.benchHint: Verify analog ADC input. Move the whammy bar to watch the live progress bar respond:
whammy.verificationDesc: When wired correctly, releasing the whammy should show a steady low or high value, and pressing the whammy bar will smoothly increase or decrease the reading.

tilt.title: 5. Star Power Tilt Sensor
tilt.description: Connect a ball tilt switch to GP11 or an I2C accelerometer to trigger Star Power / Overdrive.
tilt.intro: Tilt sensors activate Star Power / Overdrive when you tilt the guitar neck upward. Santroller supports digital ball tilt switches and I2C accelerometers.
tilt.digitalIntro: A ball tilt switch (such as the SW-520D) opens or closes when tilted at roughly 45°.
tilt.seriesTipTitle: Tip: Wire two switches in series
tilt.seriesTipDesc: To prevent false triggers from hard strumming, wire two tilt switches in series. Both switches must close simultaneously to trigger Star Power.
tilt.digitalPinGnd: Connect one pin of the tilt sensor to any GND on the Pico.
tilt.digitalPinGp: Connect the other pin to GP11 (Pin 15).
tilt.digitalMount: Mount the sensor inside the guitar body angled slightly upward towards the neck.
tilt.i2cIntro: Accelerometers measure gravitational acceleration along 3 axes for tilt detection.
tilt.i2cShared: A GH5 neck or MPR121 slider can share these SDA / SCL pins with the accelerometer; connect them in parallel.
tilt.accelDriverDesc: Add an accelerometer (ADXL345, LIS3DH or MPU-6050) on I2C (GP{{sda}} SDA / GP{{scl}} SCL) and drive tilt from its X axis.
tilt.accelBenchHint: Raw accelerometer reading (tilt the neck up and down):
tilt.accelAxisDesc: Tilt is read from the X axis, with level as no tilt and the X axis pointing straight up as full tilt. If the reading barely moves when you lift the neck, or moves the wrong way, change the axis or swap the minimum and maximum on the Tilt input in the Inputs page.
tilt.benchHint: Tilt the guitar body upward to test activation:
tilt.invertDesc: If your tilt sensor triggers when resting and turns off when lifted, toggle "Invert" in the input settings.

nav.title: 6. Start, Select & Menu Navigation
nav.description: Wire the Start and Select buttons to GP9 and GP10, and optionally configure the Home combo.
nav.intro: Start (Pause / Plus) and Select (Star Power / Minus) buttons let you navigate menus and pause songs.
nav.navGround: Find Common Ground: Follow the traces between the Start and Select contacts or use continuity mode on your multimeter. Connect the common ground to any GND pin on the Pico.
nav.startSignal: Start Button Signal: Connect the Start signal wire to GP9 (Pin 12).
nav.selectSignal: Select Button Signal: Connect the Select signal wire to GP10 (Pin 14).
nav.comboDesc: You can configure a shortcut in Santroller to map Start + Select to the Guide / Home button if your guitar lacks a dedicated guide button.
nav.benchHint: Assign pins or click Probe and press Start or Select to test:

wii-intro.intro: The Wii adapter lets you plug any controller that goes into a Wii Remote, like a Guitar Hero or Rock Band guitar, drum kit, DJ Hero turntable or Classic Controller, into a Raspberry Pi Pico and use it on PC or consoles with ultra-low latency.
wii-intro.adapterCaption: A completed Wii controller adapter powered by a Pi Pico

Soldering Iron & 4 wires
wii-intro.noDisassemblyText: Building an external adapter requires zero modifications to your controllers. Their original Wii connector plugs directly into the adapter.

wii-wiring.intro: Connect the 4 wires from your Wii female connector or breakout board to the Raspberry Pi Pico.

drum-kit.title: Direct-Wired Drum Kit
drum-kit.subtitle: Wire a drum kit's piezo pads and kick pedal to a Pico through multiplexers
drum-kit.description: Build a velocity-sensitive drum kit from piezo pads, or replace the board in a Guitar Hero or Rock Band kit, with every pad wired to a Raspberry Pi Pico through a multiplexer.

drum-intro.title: 1. Supplies & Drum Architecture
drum-intro.description: Understanding piezo velocity sensors, protection diodes, and multiplexer expansion.
drum-intro.intro: Build a custom drum kit or convert existing Guitar Hero / Rock Band drum pads using a Raspberry Pi Pico. Each pad uses a piezo, which gives a voltage pulse that grows with how hard you hit it. The Pico only has three ADC pins (GP26 - GP28), so every piezo goes through one analog multiplexer, which lets a single ADC pin read all of the pads with velocity, kick pedal included.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Piezoelectric Sensors (1 per drum pad / cymbal / kick)
1MΩ Resistors (1 per piezo to pull signal to ground)
3.3V Zener Diodes (1 per piezo, to protect the multiplexer and Pico from high voltage spikes)
Analog Multiplexer: a 74HC4051 / CD4051 (8 channels) or 74HC4067 / CD4067 (16 channels)
drum-intro.mux4051Caption: 4051 8-channel analog multiplexer pinout (Z is the common pin)
drum-intro.layoutDesc: Wire each pad's piezo to the multiplexer channel below. The guide's setup button maps the pads to these channels.
drum-intro.otherKitsTitle: Band Hero or World Tour kit?
drum-intro.otherKitsText: These kits can be converted without hardwiring piezos. For a Band Hero / Guitar Hero 5 era kit, use the Band Hero Drum Kit guide instead. For a Guitar Hero World Tour kit, use the World Tour Drum Kit guide. An e-drum kit with a 5-pin MIDI OUT port doesn't need hardwired piezos either: use the MIDI In (5-pin DIN) guide to connect its MIDI OUT to the Pico.

drum-wiring.title: 2. Piezo & Multiplexer Wiring
drum-wiring.description: Connect each piezo with a 1MΩ resistor and 3.3V zener diode to a multiplexer channel, then wire the multiplexer to the Pico.
drum-wiring.intro: Piezos generate an analog voltage pulse proportional to how hard you hit the drum pad. Each piezo gets its own resistor and zener diode, then connects to one multiplexer channel.
drum-wiring.polarityWarningText: Piezo discs are directional. Connect the outer brass ring (black wire) to Ground and the inner ceramic disc (red wire) to the multiplexer channel. If hits register weakly, swap the wires.
wiringSteps: Black Wire to Ground: Connect the outer brass ring (black wire) to a common GND.
Red Wire to the Multiplexer: Connect the inner ceramic disc (red wire) to the pad's multiplexer channel from the layout table.
1MΩ Resistor: Connect a 1MΩ resistor between the signal line and ground to pull the line low when not hit.
3.3V Zener Diode: Connect a 3.3V zener diode between signal and ground (cathode to signal, anode to ground) to clamp spikes over 3.3V.
muxSteps: Common: Connect the multiplexer's common pin (Z on a 4051, COMMON / SIG on a 4067) to GP{{com}} (Pin {{comPhysical}}, ADC0).
Select Pins: Connect S0 to GP{{s0}} (Pin {{s0Physical}}), S1 to GP{{s1}} (Pin {{s1Physical}}), and S2 to GP{{s2}} (Pin {{s2Physical}}). A 4067 also needs S3 on GP{{s3}} (Pin {{s3Physical}}).
Power: Connect VCC to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36) and GND to a Pico GND pin.
Enable & VEE: Connect the enable pin (E with a bar over it, sometimes INH) to GND so the chip is always on. A 4051 also has a VEE pin: connect it to GND too.
Channels: Channel 0 is Y0 on a 4051, and I0 on a 4067. Leave unused channels unconnected, or tie them to GND.
drum-wiring.slowText: CD40xx multiplexers switch channels more slowly than 74HC parts at 3.3V. Picking a CD part in the setup sets the multiplexer's Slow option, so the firmware waits for the reading to settle after switching channels (at the cost of slower polling). It can also be changed later on the Devices page.
drum-wiring.setupDesc: Pick your kit type and multiplexer chip. This adds the multiplexer (common on GP{{com}}, select pins on GP{{s0}}, GP{{s1}} and GP{{s2}}, plus GP{{s3}} for a 4067), switches the profile to the chosen drum kit, and maps each pad to its channel with a starting strike threshold. Pads that already have a mapping are moved to the multiplexer.
drum-wiring.setupProgress: {{mapped}} of {{total}} pads mapped to the multiplexer
drum-wiring.hitMonitorDesc: Tap the pads to verify velocity response. Each bar shows the raw reading of that pad's input, held briefly after a hit.

check.muxMissing: No multiplexer added yet (see the wiring step)
check.muxConfigured: Mux on GP{{com}} (S0 - S2: GP{{s0}}, GP{{s1}}, GP{{s2}}), {{count}} pads mapped
check.verifyPrompt: Each bar is a pad's raw reading, held briefly after a hit, so you can see how hard a hit has to be to get past its threshold.
check.tipsText: Each pad's deadzone on the Inputs page is its strike threshold (a Rock Band kick uses its trigger value instead). If a pad triggers on its own, or hitting one drum triggers an adjacent one (cross-talk), raise that pad's deadzone or debounce there.

bh-drums.title: Band Hero Drum Kit
bh-drums.subtitle: Replace the chip in a Band Hero or Guitar Hero 5 drum kit's brain with a Pico
bh-drums.description: Replace the main microcontroller in a Band Hero or Guitar Hero 5 era drum kit brain with a Raspberry Pi Pico, reading the pads from the brain's own drum chip over I2C.

bh-intro.title: Supplies & Overview
bh-intro.description: How the drum brain works, and what this conversion replaces.
bh-intro.intro: Band Hero and Guitar Hero 5 era drum kits share their brain's main board with DJ Hero turntables, Warriors of Rock guitars and Guitar Hero 5 guitars. The drum logic itself runs on its own microcontroller (an HA2005-I/SS, a rebadged PIC18F25K20), which reads the pads and streams MIDI notes to the main board over I2C. The Pico takes the main board's place: it reads that MIDI stream, and the brain's face buttons are wired straight to Pico GPIOs.
bh-intro.notPiezoTitle: You don't need the piezo drum guide
bh-intro.notPiezoText: The kit's own drum chip already reads the pads with velocity, so there is no piezo, resistor, zener diode or multiplexer wiring in this conversion. The Drum Kit & E-Drums (Piezo & Multiplexer) guide is not needed for these kits.
bh-intro.howText: Open the brain, remove the PCB with the main microcontroller from the main PCB, and connect the Pico to the I2C lines it used. The connector is labelled +V, CLK, DATA and 0V, and works the same as the DJ Hero turntable platter connection. The Pico talks to the drum chip at I2C address 0x0D.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Band Hero / Guitar Hero 5 era drum kit
Soldering Iron & Wire
bh-intro.warningTitle: This replaces the brain's main microcontroller
bh-intro.warningText: Once the main microcontroller board is removed, the kit no longer works on its own console. Keep the removed board safe if you may want to put the kit back to stock.
bh-intro.pinoutDesc: The I2C connector must use these pins. The button pins are suggestions that keep clear of GP{{sda}} / GP{{scl}}; the probe rows in the wiring step take whichever pin you actually use.

bh-wiring.title: Brain & Button Wiring
bh-wiring.description: Wire the drum chip connector to the Pico over I2C, add the driver, then wire the face buttons and optional LEDs.
bh-wiring.removalPhotoCaption: Remove the small microcontroller PCB shown on the right from the orange-outlined footprint on the main board. Leave the main board in place.
removalSteps: Remove the small microcontroller PCB from the outlined location. Leave the larger main board in place.
bh-wiring.mainBoardPhotoCaption: Orange marks the face-button headers; teal marks the four-pad drum-chip connector (+V, DATA, CLK, 0V).
buttonSteps: Button Common: The BUTTON COM / BUT COM pads are ground. Connect them to a Pico GND, so each button pulls its pin low against the Pico's pull-ups.
Left Header: Wire GUIDE/MENU, UP, DOWN, LEFT and RIGHT to free Pico GPIOs (VBAT and BUT COM are the other pads on this header).
Lower-Left Header: Wire START and BACK to free Pico GPIOs (VBAT and BUTTON COM are the other pads on this header).

Top Header: Next to the BIND label, the pads read BUTTON COM, NC, BUTTON COM, Y/TRIANGLE, X/SQUARE, B/CIRCLE, A/CROSS. Wire Y, X, B and A to free Pico GPIOs, and leave the first pad beside the BIND label and the NC pad unconnected.
Probe: Add the driver, then press Probe on each row and press that button on the brain to assign its pin. Rows for buttons you don't wire can be skipped.
bh-wiring.ledsText: LED wiring is optional. On this kit, use the +3V3 and P1-P4 pads on the removed microcontroller PCB: connect +3V3 to the Pico's 3V3(OUT), and connect P1-P4 to GPIO pins.
bh-wiring.leaveText: Do not connect VBAT, +1V6, the SPEAKER / SW header, MIC- / MIC+, or any NC pad to the Pico. Use the +V, CLK, DATA and 0V connector, button pads and BUTTON COM, and the optional LED pins for your board revision.
bh-wiring.setupDesc: Adds the Band Hero drum driver on I2C1 (GP{{sda}} / GP{{scl}}), gives the profile a MIDI channel 10 slot for it, and loads the default MIDI drum mappings. The profile is switched to a Guitar Hero drum kit unless it is already a drum kit.

wt-drums.title: World Tour Drum Kit
wt-drums.subtitle: Replace a Guitar Hero World Tour drum kit's brain with a Pico
wt-drums.description: Replace the brain of a Guitar Hero World Tour drum kit with a Raspberry Pi Pico, reading the pads over the kit's own SPI cable.

wt-intro.title: Supplies & Overview
wt-intro.description: How the kit works, and what this conversion replaces.
wt-intro.intro: In a Guitar Hero World Tour drum kit, the drum pads connect to the kit's brain (its main board) through a removable cable. The pad side reads the pads and streams MIDI notes over SPI along that cable. The Pico replaces the original brain: the cable is unplugged from the brain and connected to the Pico, which reads the MIDI stream as the SPI master. While the Pico is connected, the kit only works through the Pico.
wt-intro.notPiezoTitle: You don't need the piezo drum guide
wt-intro.notPiezoText: The kit already reads the pads with velocity, so there is no piezo, resistor, zener diode or multiplexer wiring in this conversion. The Drum Kit & E-Drums (Piezo & Multiplexer) guide is not needed for these kits.
wt-intro.howText: Unplug the cable that runs from the drum pads into the kit's original brain (main board), and connect the Pico to that cable instead. The brain's silkscreen labels its connector CS, +3V3, MOSI, 0V, MISO and CLK; use those labels to work out which wire of the cable is which. The labels are from the brain's side, which is the side the Pico takes over, so MOSI goes to the Pico's SPI TX, MISO to its SPI RX and CLK to its SPI clock.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Guitar Hero World Tour drum kit
Wire, plus a connector or a soldering iron
wt-intro.reversibleText: Nothing is cut or removed from the original brain: it is unplugged and not used while the Pico is connected. Plug the cable back into the original brain to restore the stock kit. Connecting the Pico to the cable through a connector or header keeps the cable untouched too, though soldering straight to the cable's wires also works.
wt-intro.buttonsText: The kit's face buttons are on the original brain, and this guide doesn't cover them yet. Only connect the drum cable to the Pico.
wt-intro.pinoutDesc: Connect each wire of the drum cable, identified by its label on the original brain's connector, to these Pico pins.

wt-wiring.title: Drum Cable Wiring
wt-wiring.description: Wire the drum cable to the Pico's SPI pins, then add the driver.
wt-wiring.photoCaption: The kit's original brain with the drum cable plugged in, labelled with each wire's signal (the red-striped wire is CLK)
cableSteps: Unplug the Cable: Open the kit and unplug the cable that runs from the drum pads into the original brain. Set the brain aside; it isn't used while the Pico is connected.

Identify the Wires: Use the labels beside the brain's connector (CS, +3V3, MOSI, 0V, MISO, CLK) to work out which wire of the cable is which. The ribbon's red-striped wire is CLK (SCK), and it sits on the same side at the drum end of the cable.
Connect to the Cable: A connector or header that mates with the cable leaves it untouched, or you can solder straight to the cable's wires.
CLK: Connect CLK to {{sckPin}}, the Pico's SPI clock (SCK).
MOSI: Connect MOSI to {{mosiPin}}, the Pico's SPI TX.
MISO: Connect MISO to {{misoPin}}, the Pico's SPI RX.
Add the Driver: With the Pico connected to the configurator, press Add World Tour Drum Driver.
wt-wiring.leaveText: Don't connect anything else to the Pico for this conversion. The face buttons and the rest of the original brain aren't covered by this guide yet.
wt-wiring.setupDesc: Adds the World Tour drum driver on SPI0 (CLK GP{{sck}}, MOSI GP{{mosi}}, MISO GP{{miso}}, CS GP{{cs}}, 500 kHz), gives the profile a MIDI channel 10 slot for it, and loads the default MIDI drum mappings. The profile is switched to a Guitar Hero drum kit unless it is already a drum kit.
wt-wiring.driverAdded: World Tour drum driver on CLK GP{{sck}}, MOSI GP{{mosi}}, MISO GP{{miso}}, CS GP{{cs}}, pads mapped

check.driverNotAdded: World Tour drum driver not added yet (see the wiring step)
check.brainNotDetected: Drums not detected; check the SPI wiring
check.tipsText: If the drums aren't detected, check the +3V3 and 0V wires, then check CLK, MOSI, MISO and CS against the labels on the original brain's connector (MOSI and MISO swapped is an easy mistake). If the drums are detected but a pad doesn't light up, its MIDI mappings can be adjusted on the Inputs page.

midi-din.title: MIDI In (5-pin DIN)
midi-din.subtitle: Add a MIDI IN socket for an e-drum kit, keyboard or other MIDI gear
midi-din.description: Build a small opto-isolated MIDI input so an e-drum kit, keyboard or other device with a 5-pin MIDI OUT port can drive the Pico, which then acts as a Guitar Hero or Rock Band drum kit.

din-intro.title: Supplies & Overview
din-intro.description: What the MIDI input does, and the parts the receiver circuit needs.
din-intro.intro: Most e-drum kits, keyboards and other MIDI gear have a round 5-pin DIN MIDI OUT port. With a small receiver circuit, the Pico can listen to that port and turn the notes it receives into controller inputs, so an e-drum kit can be played as a Guitar Hero or Rock Band drum kit on a console or PC. The kit keeps working as normal; the Pico only listens to its MIDI OUT.
din-intro.howText: MIDI sends its data as a current loop on pins 4 and 5 of the DIN connector. In the receiver, that current drives an H11L1 optocoupler, and the H11L1's output switches the Pico's UART RX pin. The sending device and the Pico are never electrically connected, which is what the MIDI standard asks a receiver to do. The Pico reads the stream at MIDI's 31250 baud and maps each note to a drum pad.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
H11L1 optocoupler (IC1 on the schematic)
1N914 diode
220Ω resistor (R1 on the schematic)
470Ω resistor (R2 on the schematic)
5-pin DIN MIDI socket (female)
A MIDI cable to connect the kit's MIDI OUT to the socket
Stripboard, perfboard or a breadboard, plus wire and a soldering iron
Optional: a 100nF capacitor (listed in the written guide, not shown on the schematic)
din-intro.voltageTitle: This is the 3.3V version of the circuit
din-intro.voltageText: The H11L1 is powered from the Pico's 3V3(OUT) pin, and R2 pulls its output up to 3.3V, so the Pico's RX pin never sees more than 3.3V. Don't power the H11L1 or connect R2 to VBUS or VSYS (5V): the Pico's GPIO pins are not 5V tolerant.
din-intro.keysText: This guide sets the Pico up as a drum kit. Any MIDI device with a 5-pin MIDI OUT works with the same circuit; for a keyboard used as Pro Keys, set the profile up as Pro Keys instead, then pick the key your keyboard starts at with Click to assign and press that key on the keyboard.
din-intro.glanceDesc: Every connection in the receiver, from the MIDI socket through the H11L1 to the Pico.

din-wiring.title: Circuit & Wiring
din-wiring.description: Build the optocoupler receiver, connect it to the MIDI socket and the Pico, and pick its RX pin.
din-wiring.pinCardDesc: Pick the Pico pin H11L1 pin 4 goes to. The wiring here follows it, and the MIDI input is set up on it as you pick.
din-wiring.pinApplyBtn: Set Up MIDI Input on This Pin
din-wiring.schematicCaption: The 3.3V MIDI receiver: MIDI socket on the left, H11L1 optocoupler (IC1) in the middle, Pico connections (+3.3V, RX, GND) on the right
din-wiring.schematicText: On the input side, socket pin 4 runs through R1 (220Ω) to H11L1 pin 1, and socket pin 5 goes straight to H11L1 pin 2. A diode sits across H11L1 pins 1 and 2, with its banded end on pin 1. Socket pins 1, 2 and 3 and H11L1 pin 3 are not connected. On the output side, H11L1 pin 6 goes to +3.3V, pin 5 to GND and pin 4 to the Pico's RX pin, with R2 (470Ω) pulling pin 4 up to +3.3V.
din-wiring.socketText: DIN socket pins aren't numbered in order around the circle. Going around the arc the order is 1, 4, 2, 5, 3, so pin 2 is the middle pin and pins 4 and 5 are the two either side of it. Most sockets have the numbers moulded next to the pins: check against those, and remember the order is mirrored when you look at the solder side instead of the front.
buildSteps: Find H11L1 Pin 1: Pin 1 is marked with a dot or notch on the package. Pins 1 to 3 run down one side and pins 4 to 6 come back up the other, so pin 6 is opposite pin 1.
Socket Pin 4: Connect MIDI socket pin 4 to one end of the 220Ω resistor (R1), and the other end of R1 to H11L1 pin 1.
Socket Pin 5: Connect MIDI socket pin 5 straight to H11L1 pin 2.
Diode: Connect the 1N914 across H11L1 pins 1 and 2, with its banded end (cathode) on pin 1 and its other end (anode) on pin 2. It protects the H11L1 if the signal is ever reversed.

Leave the Rest of the Socket: Socket pins 1, 2 and 3 are not connected. Pin 2 carries the cable's shield, which the sending device grounds; leaving it unconnected keeps the two devices' grounds apart.
Power: Connect H11L1 pin 6 (VCC) to the Pico's 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36), and H11L1 pin 5 (GND) to a Pico GND (Pin 38). Leave H11L1 pin 3 unconnected.
Pull-Up: Connect the 470Ω resistor (R2) between H11L1 pin 4 and 3V3(OUT).
Output: Connect H11L1 pin 4 to GP{{rx}} (Pin {{rxPhysical}}), the Pico's UART RX. You can pick a different RX pin below.
Connect the Kit: Run a MIDI cable from the kit's MIDI OUT port to the socket. The socket is the receiver's MIDI IN.
din-wiring.capText: The written guide's parts list includes a 100nF capacitor, but the schematic doesn't show one. It is optional; if you fit it, connect it between H11L1 pin 6 (VCC) and pin 5 (GND), as close to the chip as you can, as a decoupling capacitor.
din-wiring.socketTableDesc: The input side of the H11L1, powered only by the sending device.
din-wiring.picoTableDesc: The output side of the H11L1, powered by the Pico.

rows.diodeTo: Across H11L1 pins 1 and 2: banded end (cathode) to pin 1, anode to pin 2

din-setup.title: MIDI Input Setup
din-setup.description: Pick the MIDI channel your kit sends on, then set up the MIDI input.
din-setup.intro: With the receiver wired, pick the channel your kit sends on, then set up the MIDI input. Its pads get mapped to the drum kit.
din-setup.channelText: Most e-drum kits send their drums on channel 10, the General MIDI drum channel, so that is the default. If your kit's manual or MIDI settings say it uses a different channel, pick that one. The Pico only listens on the chosen channel: the profile's MIDI slot only picks up the input once a message arrives on that channel, and the pad mappings only read notes on it.
din-setup.notesText: Pads are matched by note number, using the General MIDI drum notes (for example 38 for the snare and 36 for the kick). Several notes map to each pad so most kits work straight away. If your kit sends different notes, the live test shows which notes arrive, and you can remap them on the Inputs page.
din-setup.pinText: GP1 is the default because no other guide uses it. Any of the Pico's UART RX pins works, and only the RX pin is used: MIDI in never sends anything back, so no TX pin is needed.
whatList: Drum Kit Profile: switches the profile to a Guitar Hero drum kit, unless it already emulates a Guitar Hero or Rock Band drum kit.
MIDI Input: adds a serial MIDI input on the chosen RX pin at 31250 baud (receive only, no TX pin).
MIDI Slot: gives the profile a MIDI slot on the chosen channel, and loads the default MIDI drum mappings.
Channel: moves the profile's MIDI slot and its MIDI mappings onto the chosen channel.
din-setup.cardDesc: Pick the channel, then set up the MIDI input. Changing the channel later and pressing Update moves the input and its mappings.
din-setup.pinConflict: {{pins}} already used by another device. Pick a different RX pin.
din-setup.uartInUse: UART{{block}} is already used by another device. Pick an RX pin on the other UART.
din-setup.added: MIDI input on GP{{rx}} (UART{{block}}), channel {{channel}}, pads mapped
din-setup.pinFromWiring: Reading MIDI on GP{{rx}} (UART{{block}}), the pin picked on the wiring step.

tips: Swapped Pins 4 and 5: If no notes arrive at all, socket pins 4 and 5 are the most common mistake, as the DIN numbering isn't in order. Swap the two wires and try again.
Optocoupler Orientation: Check H11L1 pin 1 is where the dot or notch is, and that the diode's banded end is on pin 1. A reversed diode shorts out the MIDI signal, so nothing gets through.
Power and RX: Check H11L1 pin 6 is on 3V3(OUT), pin 5 on GND, R2 between pin 4 and 3V3(OUT), and pin 4 on the RX pin chosen on the wiring step.
MIDI OUT, not IN: Make sure the cable runs from the kit's MIDI OUT (not MIDI IN or THRU) to the socket, and that the kit's MIDI output is turned on in its settings.
Wrong Channel: If notes arrive but the pads don't move, check the channel the notes arrive on matches the channel chosen in setup. Go back to setup and pick the kit's channel.
Unmapped Notes: If notes arrive on the right channel but a pad doesn't move, the kit sends a note the defaults don't use. Remap that pad to the note shown here on the Inputs page.
check.activityDesc: The latest notes the Pico has received, newest first.
check.notAdded: MIDI input not added yet (see the setup step)
check.waiting: No notes received yet. Hit a pad.
check.wrongChannel: Notes are arriving on channel {{got}}, but the MIDI input listens on channel {{channel}}. Go back to setup and pick channel {{got}}.

dj-turntable.title: DJ Hero Turntable Controller
dj-turntable.subtitle: Replace a DJ Hero turntable's main board with a Pico
dj-turntable.description: Replace the main board in a DJ Hero turntable (Xbox 360, PS3 or Wii) with a Raspberry Pi Pico, reading its platters, crossfader, effects dial and buttons.

tt-intro.title: 1. Supplies & Pinout Plan
tt-intro.description: Understand the I2C platters, crossfader, effects dial, and base buttons.
tt-intro.intro: Convert an original DJ Hero Turntable controller (Xbox 360, PS3, or Wii) into a low-latency USB scratch controller for DJ Hero by replacing its main board with a Raspberry Pi Pico.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
DJ Hero Turntable Controller
Soldering Iron & Wire
tt-intro.subsystemsIntro: A complete DJ Hero turntable consists of four distinct sections:
subsystems: Platter: Has its own small microcontroller that reads the spin sensor and the three platter buttons, and reports them to the base over I2C (4 wires: power, ground, SDA, SCL).
Platter Buttons: 3 buttons on the platter (Green, Red, Blue), read by the platter itself, so they need no extra wires.
Crossfader: Potentiometer with Left / Centre / Right zones, read on an ADC pin.
Base Buttons: Euphoria, Start, Select, the Xbox / PS / Home button, the D-pad, and the effects dial.
tt-intro.pinoutDesc: Recommended Raspberry Pi Pico pin connections (the platter pins are shared by both platters):

tt-wiring.title: 2. Platter & Base Wiring
tt-wiring.description: Wire the platters over I2C, then the crossfader, effects dial, and base buttons.
tt-wiring.removeBoardText: Remove the green PCB shown in the photo from the turntable base; this is the original main board that the Pico replaces. Leave the small PCBs in the platters installed. Keep the removed board safe if you may want to restore the controller to stock.
tt-wiring.mainBoardPhotoCaption: Wired DJ Hero turntable: the green PCB shown here is the main board to remove.
wiringSteps: Platters (I2C): Each platter connects to the base with 4 wires: power, ground, SDA, and SCL. Connect power to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36), ground to GND, SDA to GP{{sda}}, and SCL to GP{{scl}}. With two platters, wire both to the same four points.
Platter Buttons: Nothing to wire. The platter reads its Green, Red, and Blue buttons itself and sends them over I2C.
Crossfader: Connect the outer pins to 3V3 and GND, and the centre wiper pin to GP26 (ADC0).
Effects Dial: If it is a three-pin potentiometer, connect the outer pins to 3V3 and GND, and the wiper to GP27 (ADC1).

Base Buttons: Connect one side of each button to GND, and the other to its pin from the pinout table: Euphoria GP2, Start GP3, Select GP4, Xbox / PS / Home GP5, and the D-pad Up, Down, Left, and Right to GP6 - GP9.
tt-wiring.orientationText: The two platters answer on different I2C addresses (left 0x0E, right 0x0D), so add a platter for each side you have installed. The side is the device's Left / Right setting: it picks which address the Pico reads, and its default mappings drive the matching left or right turntable controls. If a platter only responds as the other side, switch its Left / Right setting on the Devices page and move its mappings to that side on the Inputs page.
tt-wiring.setupDesc: Add each installed platter on GP{{sda}} (SDA) / GP{{scl}} (SCL) with its default mappings, then map the base controls to the suggested pins. The profile is switched to a DJ Hero turntable if it isn't one already.
tt-wiring.applyBaseBtn: Map Base Controls to Suggested Pins
tt-wiring.scratchDesc: Spin each platter: its bar moves away from the middle while it turns and settles back in the middle when it stops.
tt-wiring.baseControlsDesc: Pick the pin each control is wired to, or press Probe and then move the control to find it.

check.scratchTestText: Spin each platter forward and backward: its velocity bar should move away from the middle in both directions and return to the middle when it stops. Slide the crossfader left and right to verify full travel.
check.title: Platters

usb-intro.intro: The Raspberry Pi Pico supports acting as a USB Host, allowing you to plug in wired USB controllers, Xbox 360 wireless receivers, Rock Band USB instruments, or donor controllers for console security authentication.

bt-receiver.title: Bluetooth Receiver
bt-receiver.subtitle: Connect PlayStation, Switch, Xbox and Wii controllers and instruments to a Pico over Bluetooth
bt-receiver.description: Turn a Pico W, or a Pico with a USB Bluetooth adapter, into a receiver for Bluetooth controllers: PS3, PS4 and PS5 pads, Switch and Xbox controllers, Wii Remotes with guitars, drums or turntables plugged in, iOS Guitar Hero Live guitars and other Santrollers. The Pico then acts as whatever each profile emulates, over USB.

bt-intro.title: Overview & Supplies
bt-intro.description: What the receiver connects to, and what you need.
bt-intro.intro: The Pico pairs with Bluetooth controllers the way a console or PC does, then shows up over USB as whatever its profiles emulate. That lets a wireless controller play on a console it was never made for, or a Wii guitar play on a PS4.
controllers: PlayStation: DualShock 3, DualShock 4 and DualSense pads, plus PS4 and PS5 Rock Band instruments.
Nintendo: Switch Pro Controllers and Joy-Con, Wii U Pro Controllers, and Wii Remotes with a guitar, drum kit, turntable or Classic Controller plugged in.
Xbox: Xbox One and Series controllers with Bluetooth.
Guitar Hero Live: the iOS guitar, which connects over Bluetooth.
Santroller: another Santroller controller set up for Bluetooth, like a wireless guitar.
Other Bluetooth gamepads, such as 8BitDo pads in Switch or Android mode.

Or a plain Pico or Pico 2 with a USB host port and a USB Bluetooth adapter plugged into it.

xbox-auth.title: Console Authentication (PS4, PS5, Xbox One / Series)
xbox-auth.subtitle: Pass auth to a real controller, an auth dongle or a harvested Xbox auth chip
xbox-auth.description: PS4, PS5, Xbox One and Xbox Series consoles only accept genuine controllers. Let Santroller pass the console's auth requests to an official controller or auth dongle on the USB Host port, or, for Xbox, to an auth chip taken from an Xbox One controller and wired over I2C.

auth-intro.title: 1. Why Consoles Need Authentication
auth-intro.description: Which consoles check for genuine controllers, and the ways to pass the check.
auth-intro.intro: Some consoles check that a controller is genuine. Santroller controllers are unofficial, so on a PS4, PS5, Xbox One or Xbox Series console Santroller passes the console's authentication requests on to something genuine: an official controller or auth dongle plugged into a USB Host port, or, for Xbox, an auth chip taken from an Xbox One controller.
consoles: Xbox 360: Santroller has the authentication keys built in, so nothing extra is needed.
Xbox One / Series S|X: An Xbox One or Series controller on the USB Host port, or an auth chip. Auth is only checked when the controller is plugged in, so the donor can be unplugged afterwards.
PS4: A DualShock 4, or a Mayflash MAGPS4 / MagicBoots PS4 dongle, on the USB Host port. Leave it plugged in while you play, as the PS4 keeps checking.
PS5 games: A Besavior P5General on the USB Host port, left plugged in. MagicBoots dongles don't work with PS5 games.
Rock Band 4 on PS4 / PS5: Doesn't need authentication in PS3 instrument mode.
Fortnite Festival: Doesn't need authentication. Use a keyboard profile instead (see the Fortnite Festival tab on the Compatibility page).
supplies: A Raspberry Pi Pico running Santroller
USB method: a USB Host port on the Pico, and an auth source for your console: an Xbox One / Series controller, a DualShock 4 or PS4 auth dongle, or a P5General for PS5
Xbox auth chip method: an auth chip removed from an Xbox One controller, fine wire and a soldering iron
auth-intro.usbTitle: Method 1: Donor controller or dongle on USB Host
auth-intro.usbBody: Plug an official controller or auth dongle for your console into a USB Host port on the Pico. When the console asks for authentication, Santroller passes the request to it and sends its answer back.
auth-intro.usbNote: Official controllers are the safe choice. Most third-party wired Xbox One controllers work too, but not every one does.
auth-intro.chipBody: Xbox One / Series only. Take the auth chip off an Xbox One controller board and wire it to the Pico's I2C pins. Santroller talks to the chip directly, so nothing needs to be plugged into a USB Host port.
auth-intro.priorityNote: You only need one of these. If both are set up, whichever is ready first answers the console.

auth-wiring.title: 2. Wire Your Auth Source
auth-wiring.description: Add a USB Host port for a donor controller, or wire an auth chip over I2C.
auth-wiring.usbIntro: The donor controller plugs into a USB Host port built from a USB socket wired to the Pico. If you've already built one with the USB Host guide, just enable it below.
auth-wiring.usbCaption: USB socket wiring: D+ and D- go straight to consecutive Pico GPIOs, with no resistors or capacitors
usbSteps: Power (Red): Solder the socket's VBUS wire to VBUS (Pin 40).
Ground (Black): Solder the socket's GND wire to any GND (Pin 38).

D- (White): Connect straight to {{dmPin}}. D+ and D- just need to be on two consecutive GPIOs, in either order: if D- is on the lower pin, turn on "D- First" for the USB Host device on the Devices page.
Plug in the donor: Connect the auth source for your console: an Xbox One / Series controller (or an Xbox Wireless Adapter with one connected), a DualShock 4 or PS4 auth dongle, or a P5General.
auth-wiring.usbGuideLink: Open the full USB Host guide
auth-wiring.usbSetupDesc: Adds a USB Host port on GP{{dp}} (D+) / GP{{dm}} (D-), the same as the USB Host guide. The donor answers the console as soon as it's plugged in, so no profile needs to be changed for it.
auth-wiring.usbConfiguredBadge: USB Host Configured on GP{{dp}} (D+) / GP{{dm}} (D-)
auth-wiring.chipIntro: The auth chip talks to the Pico over I2C, on the same I2C1 header pins the other guides use. It answers on its own address, so it can share these pins with a Wii extension, a Guitar Hero 5 neck or other I2C devices.
chipSteps: Remove the chip: Take the auth chip off an Xbox One controller board. Pin 1 is marked by the dot (GND in the pinout above).
SDA: Wire the chip's SDA pin to {{sdaPin}}.
CLK: Wire the chip's CLK pin (the I2C clock, SCL) to {{sclPin}}.
Power: Wire the chip's VCC pin to 3V3(OUT) (Pin 36), and its GND pin to any GND (Pin 38).
Reset (optional): Wire the chip's RST pin to any free GPIO, then set that pin as Reset on the Xbox One Auth Chip card on the Devices page.
auth-wiring.chipWarningTitle: Check the chip before powering it
auth-wiring.chipWarning: This guide doesn't cover where the chip sits on each Xbox One controller revision. Check the chip's marking and pin 1 dot against the pinout, double-check SDA, CLK, VCC and GND before plugging the Pico in, and only power the chip from 3.3V.
auth-wiring.chipPinoutCaption: Xbox One auth chip pinout (top view, pin 1 at the dot): GND, SDA, NC, NC, NC down the left; VCC, RST, CLK, NC, NC down the right
auth-wiring.chipSetupDesc: Adds an Xbox One Auth Chip device on I2C1. The reset pin is optional and can be set on the Devices page:
auth-wiring.chipConfiguredBadge: Auth Chip Configured on GP{{sda}} (SDA) / GP{{scl}} (SCL)
auth-wiring.devicesLink: Edit pins on the Devices page

auth-test.title: 3. Check, Save & Play
auth-test.description: Check the auth source is detected, save to the Pico, and plug into your console.
auth-test.saveText: Save the configuration to the Pico, then check the status panel shows your auth source.
consoleStepsUsb: Plug the donor controller or auth dongle into the Pico's USB Host port.
Plug the Pico into the console. Santroller picks the console's mode on its own when it detects it.
When the console starts up the controller, Santroller passes its authentication requests to the donor.
If the controller works in the console menus, authentication passed. On a PS4 or PS5, leave the donor plugged in while you play.
consoleStepsChip: Plug the Pico into the Xbox. Santroller switches to Xbox One mode on its own when it detects the console.
When the console starts up the controller, Santroller passes its authentication requests to the auth chip.
If the controller works in the console menus, authentication passed.
troubleUsb: Nothing detected: Check the USB Host wiring, that D+ and D- are on consecutive pins, and that "D- First" is enabled on the Devices page if D- is on the lower pin.
Detected but auth fails: Use an official controller or a supported dongle for that console. Most third-party Xbox One controllers work, but not every one.
Plugged in late: On an Xbox, if the donor is plugged in after the console has started the controller, Santroller reconnects to the console so it can authenticate again.
troubleChip: Chip not detected: Check SDA, SCL, power and ground. The Pico only looks for the chip when it starts, so unplug and replug the Pico after changing the wiring.
Sharing I2C pins: Other I2C devices on GP{{sda}} / GP{{scl}} are fine, but every device on those pins runs at the slowest device's speed.
auth-test.usbWaiting: USB Host Enabled, No Device Detected
auth-test.usbNotConfiguredPrompt: Go back to the Wiring step and enable the USB Host port first.
auth-test.usbVerifyPrompt: Plug the donor controller or auth dongle into the USB Host port and check it shows up here.
auth-test.connectPrompt: Connect your Pico to see the live status.
auth-test.chipNotConfiguredPrompt: Go back to the Wiring step and add the auth chip first.
auth-test.chipReadyPrompt: The Pico found the auth chip and will use it for Xbox One / Series authentication.
auth-test.chipNotDetectedPrompt: The Pico couldn't find the chip. Save, then unplug and replug the Pico. If it still isn't found, check the wiring.

console-output.title: Play on a Wii or PS2 (Console Output)
console-output.subtitle: Plug your Pico controller into a Wii Remote or a PS2 controller port
console-output.description: Wire a Wii extension plug or a PS2 controller plug to your Raspberry Pi Pico so it acts as a Wii extension or a PS2 controller on the real console, optionally with a USB host port so a USB controller can be played on the old console.

console-intro.title: Choose Your Console & Supplies
console-intro.description: Pick the console you are plugging into, and whether a USB controller should be played through it.
console-intro.intro: Console output turns the Pico into the controller itself: plugged into a Wii Remote it answers as a Wii extension (like a Guitar Hero guitar or a Classic Controller), and plugged into a PS2 it answers as a PS2 controller. Your profile's mappings are used just like they are over USB. Add a USB host port, and a USB controller plugged into the Pico can be played on the old console too.
console-intro.consoleWii: Wii (extension plug into a Wii Remote)
console-intro.usbNo: A controller wired to the Pico
console-intro.usbYes: A USB controller via USB host
console-intro.usbHelp: The USB host option adds a USB socket, so a USB controller plugged into the Pico can be played on the console. Powered from the console, it also needs a boost converter to make 5V for the socket.
console-intro.usbPowerWarningTitle: Powering from USB: leave the console's power lines off the Pico
console-intro.usbPowerWarningWii: Do not connect the plug's 3.3V (VCC) pin to the Pico. Only the signal wires and GND go to the Pico; the Pico runs from its own USB port.
console-intro.usbPowerWarningPs2: Do not connect pin 5 (3.3V) or pin 3 (7.6V rumble) to the Pico. Only the signal wires and GND go to the Pico; the Pico runs from its own USB port.
console-intro.howWii: The Wii Remote reads extensions over I2C, with the Pico answering as the extension. Until a profile takes over, the Pico shows up as a Guitar Hero guitar so the Wii Remote keeps talking to it, and as soon as the Wii Remote is talking, the profile switches to its Wii assignment list.
console-intro.howPs2: The PS2 polls its controller ports over an SPI-style bus, with the console as the master. The Pico stays silent until the console starts polling, then the profile switches to its PS2 assignment list and the Pico answers as a PS2 controller.
console-intro.rumbleTitle: Be extremely careful with the rumble wire
console-intro.rumbleText: Pin 3 of the PS2 plug is the rumble motor supply (7.6V). Never connect it to the Pico. If your plug has a rumble wire, cut it short and insulate it properly, as you can easily blow the rumble fuse inside the console if it touches something it shouldn't.
console-intro.coloursTitle: Do not rely on the wire colours
console-intro.coloursText: Manufacturers are all over the place with Wii extension cable colours, so check each wire with a multimeter against the plug pinout. Some cables use green as ground and black as 3.3V, and some (even from Guitar Hero guitars) already short device detect to 3.3V inside the cable.
console-intro.diodeTitle: Power goes through a Schottky diode
console-intro.diodeText: The console's 3.3V line feeds the Pico through a Schottky diode. It protects the console if the Pico is plugged into USB at the same time; never wire the console's power straight to the Pico.
suppliesWii: A Wii extension plug (the end that plugs into the Wii Remote)
suppliesPs2: A PS2 controller plug (the end that plugs into the console)
suppliesConsolePower: A Schottky diode (rated for more than 10V reverse voltage)
suppliesUsbPower: A USB power source for the Pico (a phone charger, power bank or PC) and a USB cable for the Pico's own USB port
suppliesBoost: An MT3608 boost converter module (3.3V up to 5V for the USB socket)
suppliesUsb: A USB extension cable cut in half (keep the socket end) or a USB socket breakout
console-intro.profileDesc: The console sees the controller type your active profile emulates.
console-intro.wiiTypesHint: Guitar Hero guitars, Guitar Hero drums, DJ Hero turntables and Taiko drums are sent as those extensions. Every other profile type is sent as a Classic Controller.
console-intro.ps2TypesHint: PS2 output supports Gamepad, Guitar Hero guitar, Taiko, pop'n music, beatmania, GuitarFreaks and DrumMania profiles.
console-intro.ps2UnsupportedTitle: This profile type has no PS2 output
console-intro.ps2UnsupportedText: The active profile emulates a {{type}}, which the firmware has no PS2 report for, so the console would get no inputs. Switch the profile to one of the supported types on the Inputs page.

console-wiring.title: Wire the Console Plug
console-wiring.description: Wire the plug's signals and power to the Pico, then add console output to your config.
console-wiring.plugCaptionWii: Wii extension plug pinout, looking into the plug
console-wiring.plugCaptionPs2: PS2 controller plug pinout (pin 1 DATA on the left, pin 9 ACK on the right)
wiiSteps: SDA: Connect the plug's SDA pin to {{sda}}.
SCL: Connect the plug's SCL pin to {{scl}}.
Ground: Connect the plug's GND pin to any Pico GND (e.g. Pin 38).
Device detect: If your plug doesn't already connect device detect to 3.3V inside the cable, connect device detect to the plug's 3.3V pin. The Wii Remote only reads the extension while detect is high.
ps2Steps: Pin 1, DATA (Brown): Connect to {{data}}. The Pico sends its button data to the console on this line.
Pin 2, COMMAND (Orange): Connect to {{command}}. The console sends its commands to the Pico on this line.
Pin 3, Rumble 7.6V: Do not connect. Cut it short and insulate it.
Pin 4, GND (Black): Connect to any Pico GND (e.g. Pin 38).
console-wiring.ps2ColoursNote: Wire colours vary between cables, so check each one against the plug pinout with a multimeter.
wiiPower: 3.3V: Connect the plug's 3.3V (VCC) pin to the Pico's VSYS (Pin 39) through the Schottky diode, with the diode's stripe (cathode) facing VSYS.
ps2Power: Pin 5, 3.3V (Red): Connect to the Pico's VSYS (Pin 39) through the Schottky diode, with the diode's stripe (cathode) facing VSYS.
Never use pin 3 (7.6V rumble) to power the Pico.
console-wiring.usbPowerTitle: Power from the Console (with USB Host)
console-wiring.usbPowerIntro: USB controllers need 5V, so the console's 3.3V is boosted to 5V and fed into VBUS, which also powers the USB socket. We recommend an MT3608 boost converter module. These are adjustable, so set the output to 5V with a multimeter (turn the small trim pot) before connecting it to the Pico.
usbSupplyPower: Power the Pico from its own USB port, using a phone charger, power bank or PC.
Ground: the plug's GND must still connect to Pico GND (from the signal steps above), so the console and Pico share a ground.
No diode or boost converter is needed. With a USB host port, the socket's VBUS wire takes its 5V from the Pico's VBUS (Pin 40).
wiiUsbPower: Boost input: Connect the plug's 3.3V (VCC) pin to the boost converter's voltage input.
Boost output: Connect the boost converter's 5V output to the Pico's VBUS (Pin 40) through the Schottky diode, with the diode's stripe (cathode) facing VBUS.
Boost ground: Connect the boost converter's ground to Pico GND.
ps2UsbPower: Boost input: Connect pin 5, 3.3V (Red) to the boost converter's voltage input.
Boost output: Connect the boost converter's 5V output to the Pico's VBUS (Pin 40) through the Schottky diode, with the diode's stripe (cathode) facing VBUS.
Boost ground: Connect the boost converter's ground to Pico GND.
Never use pin 3 (7.6V rumble) to power anything.
usbSteps: VBUS (Red): Connect the socket's red wire to the Pico's VBUS (Pin 40).
Ground (Black): Connect the socket's black wire to any Pico GND.
D+ (Green): Connect the socket's green wire to {{dp}}.

D- (White): Connect the socket's white wire to {{dm}}. D+ and D- can be swapped as long as they stay on consecutive pins; if you swap them, turn on "D- First" for the USB Host device on the Devices page.
console-wiring.usbCaption: USB socket wiring: D+ and D- go straight to consecutive Pico GPIOs, with no resistors or capacitors
console-wiring.usbNoPins: No free pair of consecutive pins was found for D+ / D-. Free up two pins, or add a USB host port on the Devices page.
console-wiring.setupDescWii: Adds Wii extension emulation on {{sda}} (SDA) / {{scl}} (SCL), then adds a Wii Remote assignment list to the top of the active profile so the profile switches to it whenever the Wii Remote is talking.
console-wiring.setupDescPs2: Adds PS2 controller emulation on the pins above, then adds a PS2 assignment list to the top of the active profile so the profile switches to it whenever the console is polling.
console-wiring.setupDescUsb: The USB host port is added on {{dp}} (D+) / {{dm}} (D-), and its USB controller slot goes into both the USB list and the console's list so they share the same mappings.
console-wiring.deviceMissing: Console output device not added yet
console-wiring.listMissing: The active profile has no assignment list for this console yet
console-wiring.usbSlotMissing: The console's assignment list has no USB controller slot yet
console-wiring.conflictText: {{pins}} are already used by another device. Free them up on the Devices page, or add the console output there on different pins.

console-test.title: Save & Play on the Console
console-test.description: Save the config to the Pico, then plug it into the console.
console-test.saveText: Save the config to the Pico's flash before you unplug it from the PC, so it keeps the console output settings.
console-test.expectTitle: What to Expect on the Console
wiiExpect: Plug in: Plug the extension plug into the Wii Remote and turn it on.
Detection: The Wii Remote reads the extension, and the profile switches to its Wii assignment list as soon as the Wii Remote starts talking.
Type: Games see the controller type shown on the right.
ps2Expect: Plug in: Plug the PS2 plug into a controller port with the console on.
Detection: The Pico stays silent until the console polls the port, then the profile switches to its PS2 assignment list and the Pico answers as a PS2 controller.
Type: Games see the controller type shown on the right. Changing the profile's type makes the Pico briefly disconnect so the game sets the controller up again.
console-test.usbExpect: USB host: Plug a supported USB controller into the socket. Most wired controllers work, but things like the Xbox 360 Play & Charge kit won't work over USB.
console-test.liveHint: When powering from USB, or from the console with the diode fitted, the Pico can stay plugged into your PC while it is plugged into the console, so the status here shows when the console starts talking.
console-test.notConfiguredPrompt: Go back to the Wiring step and set up console output first.
console-test.connectPrompt: Connect the Pico to see live status.
console-test.detectedBadge: Console Is Talking to the Pico

xbox360-rf.title: Xbox 360 Wireless Receiver (RF Module)
xbox360-rf.subtitle: Connect Xbox 360 wireless controllers and instruments to a Pico through an original RF module
xbox360-rf.description: Repurpose an authentic Xbox 360 RF module (Original/Fat or Slim) as an ultra-low latency wireless receiver for Xbox 360 controllers with sync and Ring of Light support.

rf-intro.title: 1. Supplies & Architecture Overview
rf-intro.description: Understand how the Xbox 360 RF module connects via USB and two-wire serial bus.
rf-intro.modelSelectLabel: Select Your Xbox 360 RF Module Hardware Revision:
rf-intro.fatPreviewCaption: Xbox 360 Original / Fat RF module connector pinout
rf-intro.slimPreviewCaption: Xbox 360 Slim RF module connection scheme
rf-intro.intro: The Xbox 360 front RF module contains an authentic Microsoft 2.4GHz wireless receiver for Xbox 360 controllers. It communicates controller inputs via standard USB lines, while LED Ring of Light animations, power commands, and controller pairing/sync are driven over a proprietary 2-wire serial bus (Data and Clock).
rf-intro.voltageWarningText: Xbox 360 RF modules operate strictly on 3.3V logic and 3.3V power! NEVER connect 5V to the module VCC pin. The Raspberry Pi Pico 3V3 OUT (Pin 36) provides clean 3.3V power, and all Pico GPIOs run at 3.3V logic.
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Xbox 360 RF module (Original 'Fat' model RF01/Rev H or Slim model)
Soldering iron, flux, and fine wire (28-30 AWG)
Optional: 1x tactile button for physical hardware sync (if not using software sync)
rf-intro.twoInterfacesText: To use the module completely, you wire two distinct interfaces:
twoInterfacesList: USB Interface (D+, D-, GND): The module's built-in wireless receiver carries the controller data over USB, so it connects to a Santroller USB host port on GP{{dp}} (D+) / GP{{dm}} (D-).
Serial Control Bus (Data, Clock, Sync): Connects to Pico GPIOs so Santroller can send sync commands, cycle LED ring animations, and trigger pairing.
rf-intro.architectureOverviewDesc: Summary of connections from the RF module to the Raspberry Pi Pico:
rf-intro.descPower: Powers the RF transceiver chip and LEDs (strictly 3.3V)
rf-intro.descUsb: Carries wireless controller data to the Pico's USB host port (D+ and D- on two consecutive GPIOs)
rf-intro.descSerialData: Command data sent from the Pico to the module (one way)
rf-intro.descSerialClock: Clock driven by the module; the Pico shifts each command bit out on it
rf-intro.descSync: Optional sync button pin (active low to ground)

rf-wiring.title: 2. Module Pinout & Wiring
rf-wiring.description: Step-by-step soldering instructions for your chosen module.
rf-wiring.usbNoteTitle: USB D+ / D- Go to the Pico USB Host Port
rf-wiring.usbNoteText: The module's controller data arrives over USB, so its D+ and D- lines are wired like the socket in the USB Host Port guide: D+ to GP{{dp}} and D- to GP{{dm}}. The two pins must be consecutive, in either order (turn on "D- First" on the Devices page if D- is on the lower pin). No resistors or capacitors are needed. Adding the module on the right adds the USB host port too, and its pins can be changed there.
rf-wiring.driverDesc: Adds the RF module on GP{{data}} (data), GP{{clock}} (clock) and GP{{sync}} (sync), and the USB host port its receiver uses on GP{{dp}} (D+) / GP{{dm}} (D-). The pins can be changed once they're added, and the wiring follows them.
rf-wiring.driverAdded: RF Module & USB Host Port Added

rf-fat.title: 2. Wiring the Original / Fat RF Module (RF01 / Rev H)
rf-fat.description: Pinout diagrams and test points for the original Xbox 360 'Fat' RF board.
rf-fat.intro: The original Xbox 360 'Fat' RF module (commonly Rev H / RF01) uses a 9-pin two-row connector on the back. You can solder either directly to the connector pins or to the convenient circular test points located on the rear of the PCB.
rf-fat.connectorCaption: Xbox 360 Fat RF module connector pinout (rear view)
rf-fat.testPointsDesc: If the connector pins are difficult to solder, you can use the marked copper test pads on the back of the board:
rf-fat.testPointsCaption: Rear PCB test points: TP18 (3.3V), TP9/TP10 (GND), TP14 (D+), TP13 (D-), TP16 (Data), TP15 (Clock)
wiringSteps: 3.3V Power: Solder Top Pin 1 (or TP18) to Pico Pin 36 (3V3 OUT).
Ground: Solder Top Pin 4 or Bottom Pin 4 (or TP9 / TP10) to Pico Pin 38 (GND).
USB D+: Solder Top Pin 3 (or TP14) to Pico {{dpPin}}, the USB host D+ pin.
USB D-: Solder Top Pin 2 (or TP13) to Pico {{dmPin}}, the USB host D- pin. D+ and D- just need to be on consecutive GPIOs, in either order (see the USB Host guide).
Serial Data: Solder Bottom Pin 2 (or TP16) to an unused Pico GPIO (e.g. GP{{data}}).
Serial Clock: Solder Bottom Pin 3 (or TP15) to an unused Pico GPIO (e.g. GP{{clock}}).
Sync Button (Optional): Solder Bottom Pin 1 to a GPIO if you want a physical sync button, or leave it unconnected and use Santroller's built-in software sync button.
rf-fat.pinoutTableTitle: Fat RF Module Pinout & Test Points
rf-fat.pinoutTableDesc: Reference pin mappings for the original Xbox 360 module:

rf-slim.title: 2. Wiring the Xbox 360 Slim RF Module
rf-slim.description: Connector pinout and wiring diagram for the Xbox 360 Slim RF board.
rf-slim.intro: The Xbox 360 Slim RF module uses a single compact internal connector. It operates on the same 3.3V serial protocol as the Fat module, but with an updated startup handshake and custom pin arrangement.
rf-slim.schemeCaption: Xbox 360 Slim RF module pinout and connection scheme
wiringSteps: 3.3V Power: Solder bottom-row Pin 12 (Orange wire) to Pico Pin 36 (3V3 OUT).
Ground: Solder the large mounting pad beside the connector (Black wire) to Pico Pin 38 (GND) and your USB shield/GND.
USB D+ (Green): Solder top-row Pin 6 (Green wire) to Pico {{dpPin}}, the USB host D+ pin.
USB D- (Grey/White): Solder top-row Pin 5 (Grey/White wire) to Pico {{dmPin}}, the USB host D- pin. D+ and D- just need to be on consecutive GPIOs, in either order (see the USB Host guide).
Serial Data: Solder top-row Pin 2 (Pink wire) to Pico GP{{data}}.
Serial Clock: Solder top-row Pin 3 (Cyan/Blue wire) to Pico GP{{clock}}.
Sync Button: Solder bottom-row Pin 13 (Yellow wire) to Pico GP{{sync}} (or an optional physical push-button to ground).
rf-slim.syncPinNoteText: The Slim RF module requires a dedicated initialisation sequence to illuminate the LEDs and initiate the pairing sweep. Santroller natively handles this when 'Slim' is selected under the Xbox 360 RF device settings.

rf-sync.title: 3. Sync Your Controllers
rf-sync.description: Sync your Xbox 360 wireless controllers to the module.
rf-sync.intro: Now connect your Pico and sync each wireless controller to the module. The next step makes a profile for each kind of controller you'll use.
rf-sync.syncInstructionsTitle: How to Pair Your Xbox 360 Controller
syncSteps: Open the Santroller Configurator and connect to your Pico via WebHID.

Check the module and its USB host port are added (the wiring step adds them, or use the button on the right). The module uses Data GP{{data}}, Clock GP{{clock}} and Sync GP{{sync}}, and the receiver GP{{dp}}/GP{{dm}}.
Click the 'Sync Controller' button in Santroller (or press your wired sync button). The LEDs on the module will begin the rotation animation.
Turn on your Xbox 360 wireless controller and hold its top sync button until its ring also spins.
Within seconds, the controller will be assigned to Player 1 and the quadrant LED will remain solidly lit.

rgb-leds.title: Addressable RGB & Fret LEDs (WS2812B / APA102)
rgb-leds.subtitle: Fret Illumination & Game Sync Animations
rgb-leds.description: Add addressable RGB LEDs to your guitar or drum kit that light up on button presses and sync with Star Power in games like YARG.

led-intro.title: 1. Supplies & LED Wiring Scheme
led-intro.description: Overview of addressable RGB LEDs, power distribution, and protection resistors.
led-intro.intro: Add RGB LEDs or addressable LED strips (APA102, SK9822, WS2812B) to your controller. Supports reactive lighting on button presses, idle animations, and game integrations.
led-intro.inlineText: If you only want each fret to light up while it is pressed, ordinary single-colour LEDs can be wired in line with the fret switches instead. They are switched by the frets themselves, are not addressable, and need no LED device in Santroller, so the rest of this guide does not apply to them. Each LED needs its own current-limiting resistor sized for that LED (use an LED resistor calculator).
led-intro.inlineCaption: Inline single-colour LEDs lit by their fret switches
led-intro.schematicCaption: Inline fret LED schematic (not for addressable LEDs): size each resistor for your LED
supplies: Raspberry Pi Pico 1 or Pico 2
Addressable RGB LEDs (APA102 / SK9822 DotStar or WS2812B NeoPixels)
330Ω to 470Ω Resistor (in series with the data line, close to the first LED, to damp ringing and reflections on the wire and protect the LED's data input)
1000µF Capacitor (across 5V power and ground to smooth out sudden current draws)
Recommended: 74AHCT125 (or 74HCT245) level shifter, or a 1N4001 diode for the first LED's power (see the 3.3V logic note)
Soldering Iron & Wire
led-intro.levelShiftText: WS2812B and APA102 LEDs powered from 5V VBUS expect a logic high of about 0.7 × VDD (around 3.5V), but the Pico's GPIOs only output 3.3V. It often works anyway, but can flicker or glitch. For reliable data, run the data (and APA102 clock) line through a 5V level shifter such as a 74AHCT125 powered from VBUS, or power just the first LED from 5V through a diode (e.g. 1N4001): its supply drops to about 4.3V, so 3.3V counts as high, and it re-drives the data to the rest of the chain at full 5V levels.
led-intro.pinoutDescWs2812: Pico connections for WS2812B LEDs (driven by PIO, so GP{{data}} is just a free pin; any GPIO works):
led-intro.pinoutDescApa102: Pico connections for APA102 / SK9822 LEDs (these need the hardware SPI pins below):
led-intro.apa102PinNote: APA102 needs a hardware SPI clock and data (TX) pair on the same SPI block. No pair on the Pico is free of every other guide: GP18 (SPI0 SCK) / GP19 (SPI0 TX) is used because it only shares pins with the optional GH5 neck / Wii extension I2C bus. If you use either of those, change the LED or I2C pins on the Devices page.

led-wiring.title: 2. Solder LEDs & Data Line
led-wiring.description: Connect power from VBUS, chain LEDs in series, and add inline protection.
wiringSteps: 5V Power: Connect the 5V line of your LED strip or fret LEDs to VBUS (Pin 40) on the Pico.
Ground: Connect the ground line to any GND (Pin 38).
Capacitor: Solder a 1000µF capacitor across 5V and GND close to the first LED (mind the polarity).

Data Line: Solder a 330Ω to 470Ω resistor inline between {{dataPin}} and the Data In (DIN) pin of the first LED, placing it close to the LED. It damps ringing on the wire and protects the LED's data input.
Chaining LEDs: Connect the Data Out (DOUT) of the first LED to the Data In (DIN) of the next, until all LEDs are connected in series.
wiringStepsApa102: 5V Power: Connect the 5V line of your LED strip or fret LEDs to VBUS (Pin 40) on the Pico.
Ground: Connect the ground line to any GND (Pin 38).
Capacitor: Solder a 1000µF capacitor across 5V and GND close to the first LED (mind the polarity).
Data Line: Solder a 330Ω to 470Ω resistor inline between {{mosiPin}}, SPI TX and the Data In (DI) pin of the first LED, placing it close to the LED to damp ringing and protect the LED's input.
Clock Line: Solder a second 330Ω to 470Ω resistor inline between {{sckPin}}, SPI SCK and the Clock In (CI) pin of the first LED.
Chaining LEDs: Connect Data Out (DO) and Clock Out (CO) of each LED to Data In (DI) and Clock In (CI) of the next, until all LEDs are connected in series.

supportedHardware.title: Supported Hardware
supportedHardware.subtitle: Microcontrollers, USB devices, sensors and accessories that work with Santroller.
supportedHardware.alertBody: Santroller 2 runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico (RP2040 or RP2350). You can wire buttons, switches and LEDs straight to the GPIO pins, read Wii, PS1/PS2, SNES/NES and N64/GameCube controllers over their original connectors, or use the USB Host port for controllers, wireless dongles and auth devices.
supportedHardware.cloneWarningTitle: Watch out for fake "Pico W" boards
supportedHardware.cloneWarningBody: A lot of cheap "Pico W" boards on AliExpress and similar sites swap the CYW43439 wireless chip for an ESP8266 or ESP8285. Those chips are Wi-Fi only and have no Bluetooth, so their built-in wireless won't work for any Santroller Bluetooth features, including wireless controllers and Wii Remote emulation. Like a regular Pico, they can still use Bluetooth through a supported USB Bluetooth dongle. A genuine Pico W / Pico 2 W has a silver metal shield over the wireless chip with the Raspberry Pi logo on it.

PIO is used for the USB host port and console controller protocols

520 KB SRAM

Uses the same Santroller firmware build for Pico 2 and Pico 2 W

details: Wii Remote emulation: play Guitar Hero, Band Hero and DJ Hero on an unmodified Wii / Wii U with retail discs
Can be used as a low-latency Bluetooth transmitter inside a wireless guitar
Pairs with a second Pico acting as the receiver
Can run off a battery on VSYS, with a Schottky diode for reverse protection
pico_w_wireless.warning: Some cheap AliExpress "Pico W" boards use an ESP8285 / ESP8266 instead of the CYW43439. Those are Wi-Fi only and have no Bluetooth, so their built-in wireless won't work (a USB Bluetooth dongle still does). Genuine boards have a silver metal shield over the wireless chip marked "Raspberry Pi".

mcu_legacy_uno_mega.warning: This board only runs the old Santroller 1 firmware, which may have bugs and is missing a lot of newer features. For new builds, use a Pico or Pico 2 instead.

details: Adds Wii Remote emulation to a regular (non-W) Pico for Wii Guitar Hero and DJ Hero
